slides.sub: Two ways a trend dies. Two different trades.

slides.title: The iceberg: size at one price
slides.body: Sellers keep hitting 24,480. The footprint shows 1,450 on the bid at that single price, while every other tick trades a few hundred.

slides.title: The DOM gives it away
slides.body: The bid at 24,480 never shows more than 60 lots, yet 1,450 trade there. Each time it is hit, it refreshes.
slides.tip: Traded volume far above displayed size = hidden passive buyer. Aggression without progress is absorption.

slides.title: Exhaustion: nobody left to sell
slides.body: Now the opposite. At the low, volume dries up: a handful of contracts at the extreme. Sellers didn't meet a wall, they ran out of fuel.

footprint.label: Low prints 8 x 20: the move ran out of sellers

slides.title: Same stop, different trade
slides.body: Iceberg: a defended level. Buy the reclaim, stop one tick below the iceberg. Exhaustion: a weak low with no defender, often revisited later.
slides.tip: Confirm both with delta: it must flip positive and price must close back above the level.

caption:
Iceberg or EXHAUSTION? Who really stopped the move 🧊

A selloff can stop for two opposite reasons. An iceberg is a hidden passive buyer: huge volume at one price, far above what the DOM displays, and price can't trade through it. Exhaustion is the absence of sellers: volume dries up at the low with tiny prints. They look the same on a candle chart, but they are different trades.

1️⃣ Big volume at one price, no progress = iceberg (defended level)
2️⃣ Traded size far above displayed size on the DOM = hidden order refilling
3️⃣ Tiny volume at the extreme = exhaustion (weak low, often revisited)
4️⃣ In both cases wait for delta to flip and price to reclaim the level
